title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 4
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of living an ethical life, which is closely tied to the Buddhist path of the Eightfold Path. To cultivate this path, one must develop qualities like honesty, courage, and self-awareness through mindfulness, effort, and concentration. Ultimately, this leads to the practice of Right Concentration, where a clear and focused mind is cultivated through meditation, allowing for a deeper understanding of emptiness and the cultivation of kindness and compassion in daily life.

sentences.text: Good evening and thank you for coming on such a beautiful summer night.
I'm quite sure that there are many things to do and much fun to be had, and you're here, so welcome to part four of our Dharma Talk series on the Four Noble Truths.
The teaching that is for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world.
I hope that hearing about the Four Noble Truths may have inspired you to investigate how they apply to your life and to your heart.
We all know that ethical conduct is important on different levels.
Society as a whole functions with the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world.
We all know what ethical conduct is, although how often do we think about it or analyze ethics, specifically within our own lives and not as judgments applied to others or what we see in the news.
How far is ethical conduct a part of our active ongoing practice?
It would be great if we could see ethical conduct as a solid something, but life is full of gray areas, full of compromises, circumstances and conditions we cannot control.
On top of this, each one of us is full of unexamined motivations and conditioned behaviors.
We are driven by our desires and our dislikes, and we tend to deceive ourselves; we are kind of ignorant.
With all of this going on, we better be willing to look at our conduct with honesty, and that, my friends, takes courage.
The consequences of our conduct, with seamless, clear eyes, is not so easy to look at at times, and looking once is not it either.
This practice is a continuous exploration.
Let us not get stuck in theory, in norms, in our conditioning.
Instead, let us look at life in all its complexity and beauty and be open to radical reality.
I hope that we all agree on this desire for ethical conduct, ethical life, less suffering for ourselves and others.
The Eightfold Noble Path has the signposts for it.
We could spend the rest of the year talking about nothing else, and I wonder if we would do more than scratch the surface.
So I hope that you and I, all of us, will engage with the Four Noble Truth on our own; the only way we can do it anyway.
It needs to be an active part of our practice.

I came up with some suggestions, and please feel free to add your own: one, practicing with the Truth as a whole overriding principle, or by practicing by taking on a small piece and picking it apart some more.
Number three I came up with was increasing our understanding of our own conduct and its consequences in an intentional manner.
Also, it is good to remember that we will stumble and crash.
The Way has many obstacles and potholes, and we create some more.
So, what does the world say to all of this?
Preparing for this talk, I wanted to look up the book, *The Meditative Way, Readings in the Theory and Practice of Buddhist Meditation*, by Roderick Bucknell and Chris Kang.
I put that in to the Amazon search bar, and yes, the book did come out as the top result.
It had one four-star review.
However, hit number two was 115, four and a half star reviews was *Dirty Cowboys*, the Spencer Sisters.
I tried to figure out how that logarithm came together, but it gave me brain cramps.
That said, let us look at the Eightfold Path again with the Buddha's words.

Because it's the noble truth of the Way leading to the end of suffering, it is the Noble Eightfold Path that is Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration.
Last week we heard about the wisdom part of the Path, which is Right View and Right Intention.
The third one, Right Speech, is one of the moral virtues.

Tonight we will complete the moral virtues, Right Action and Right Livelihood, and also the third category, which addresses meditation and includes Right Effort, Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration.
So the fourth factor is Right Action.
There is so much to be said about it that I made it just one short paragraph because there is not really getting into it in this short amount of time.
The Buddha said, and what is Right Action?
This is Right Action: abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct.
This is Right Action.
We all realize that when we do not practice Right Action, we cause harm.
So the question to ask is, what harm did I cause to myself, and how did I harm the other person?
That is a start.
Right Livelihood is next.
The early texts state Right Livelihood as avoiding and abstaining from wrong livelihood.
This virtue is further explained as living from begging, but not accepting everything and not possessing more than is strictly necessary.
For lay Buddhists, which is all of us, this precept requires that the livelihood avoids causing suffering to sentient beings.
And suffering includes cheating them or harming or killing them in any way.
The texts speak of not trading in weapons, in living beings, meat, alcoholic drink or poison.
The raising and trading of cattle for slaughter seen in this light is a breach of Right Livelihood.
Buddhist communities in the East actually lack the mass slaughterhouses found in Western countries.
Yet, please remember that the Buddha took all offerings equally, and all offerings that mean meat also.
So now we have made it through the third category, meditation.
The first meditation factor is Right Effort.
Right Effort deals with wholesome and unwholesome mental states, such as desire and aversion.
It asks for effort to prevent the arising and to lead to the ending of unwholesome states.
Essential desires are restrained by minding the sense faculties.
Ill will is to be eliminated by effort.
And ill will includes all forms of aversion, hatred, anger, resentment towards anything or anyone.
At the same time, we need to encourage the positive mental states we already possess.
This is very important.
We humans are such interesting creatures.
On one hand, we think so highly of ourselves and we become so self-protective if we hear any type of criticism.
And yet, we really have a problem with seeing how wonderful we can be and how wonderful we are, well, not all the time.
But the seeds are there, and there are some tender little sprouts of wonderfulness that need nourishing.
And let's believe that we have some sturdy trees we can hold on to when we feel shaky.
We do need to remember not to use the Dharma to beat ourselves up, but also to lift ourselves up.
Right mindfulness, now that's a pretty loaded word nowadays, bought and sold wherever you look, but that would be a whole talk in itself.
So that mindfulness comes originally from the *Satipitana Sutta*.
It is also called the Four Foundations of Mindfulness or the Four Domains.
The Four Domains are body, feelings, mind and phenomena.
Right mindfulness is to be diligently aware, mindful and attentive with regard to the activities in the body and off the body.
Sensations or feelings.
Third is the activities of the mind, and fourth is phenomena or Dharma, which covers ideas, thoughts, conceptions and things.
Establishing the Four Foundations is not theory; it is practice.
In the Sutta actually there are activities and very precise meditation instructions.
Practicing right mindfulness with regard to the body, we can regulate our responses to events, people and situations.
With the awareness we do have a warning process to detect fight, flight and freeze and make more conscious choices instead of knee-jerk reactions.
In regard to feelings, one should be clearly aware of how they appear and disappear within oneself.
A brief side note, in the *Satipatana*, the word feelings does not mean emotions; it means simply likes and dislikes.
Watching the mind, one should be aware whether one's mind is desirous or not, given to hatred or not, deluded or not, distracted or concentrated, and so on.
In this way one should be aware of all movements of the mind, especially how they arise and disappear and how we try to hold on to states in a certain shape.
One should observe ideas, thoughts, concepts and things.
One should know their nature and how they get destroyed.
These four forms of mental cultivation with specific meditations are treated in detail in the *Satipatana Sutta*.
We have now arrived at the last of the factors of the path, right concentration.
According to Bhikkhu Bodhi, the right concentration factor is reaching a one-pointedness of mind in unifying all mental factors.
But it is not the same as a thief breaking into a house.
That thief also achieves one-pointed concentration; he's watching all ears and he's watching everything he does because he wants to get in and out undetected.
The difference is that the thief only has one mindful thing going in his life: breaking into houses.
The demand on us is somewhat larger.
Right concentration in Buddhism is a state of awareness without any specific object or subject, and ultimately one arrives at emptiness.
Buddhist literature contains descriptions and practices for stages of meditation or jhanas, and traditionally that was also included in right concentration.
However, our Mahayana Zen view tells us to sit in the middle of all of it, to see what is going on and to see what's going on in our mind.
So this concludes the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
However, in my studies I came across some painful notes too.
Many of the ancient texts are very misogynistic.
For one, the texts as translated speak of the monk, the noble one in male form, period.
Being female, being a woman was specifically considered a hindrance.
We can acknowledge this as a historical fact.
Also in the West today we may see glass ceilings, and that being male continues to impact wages, opportunities and privilege.
However, to this day monastic institutions for women in the East suffer greatly from this disparity.
People see to be prayed for by monks as bringing greater merit than by nuns.
It is painful to consider this, that this continues on to this day.
So if you ever see an opportunity to level out the playing field, please do so.
And also in conclusion, please let us try to use the teachings in their intended way.
Pay respect to the Buddhas and the ancestors and to ourselves, to you and me, by and through practicing the Dharma.
Our habit is to take what the senses, the aggregates, give us.
We turn it into something permanent that we either like, dislike or don't care about.
So that means we take our sense input and we turn it into suffering mostly.
The good side is that we can stop clinging to these habits.
We can be dispassionate about our habits.
We can be honest about our deeds and their consequences and develop the noble eightfold path within us to find a mind still and steady.
And it is up to each and every one of us to do that for ourselves.
The Dalai Lama often says, "My religion is kindness."
So if you are asking yourself what to do next, how to decide, where to go with your actions, remember kindness, unselfish kindness, and leave judgments behind.
Without love, there is no noble truth, no eightfold path, no bodhisattva way, no precepts.
